One evening, when her husband entered the room unexpectedly, she was startled so much that she dropped the book she was reading. The assault has also seeped into Eleanor's daily routines and social life. She avoids certain areas where the attack occurred, and even familiar paths now feel dangerous. This avoidance extends to her work as well; although retired, she volunteers occasionally at legal aid clinics. However, these visits have become increasingly rare due to her fear of being alone or in unfamiliar environments. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has strained her relationships. Her husband, while supportive, feels perplexed by Eleanor's sudden change. He has noticed her constant vigilance and has tried to reassure her that she is safe at home. However, his efforts often fall short, as the fear remains deeply ingrained in her psyche. Despite her best attempts to carry on with daily life, Eleanor's fears have begun to take a toll. She finds herself avoiding social gatherings and even feels hesitant about venturing out alone. This constant state of hypervigilance has left her feeling exhausted and anxious, making it difficult for her to engage in activities that once brought her joy. It was during one particularly harrowing day when she felt overwhelmed by her symptoms that Eleanor decided to seek help. She is most afraid that her fears will continue to consume her life, leaving little room for the relationships and activities she values. However, she also harbors a glimmer of hope-that with professional support, she can reclaim some sense of safety and peace. In the present moment, Eleanor's primary goal is to regain control over her daily life and alleviate the persistent fear that haunts her. She hopes that therapy will help her understand why these fears persist and provide tools to manage them effectively. As she takes this step towards healing, Eleanor holds onto the belief that with time and support, she can reclaim a sense of normalcy and security in her everyday experiences.

Lily, a 29-year-old South Eastern Asian woman, has been a combat pilot for several years. Her life took an unexpected turn when her younger brother was killed in a training accident while serving with the military. The event occurred shortly after she had returned from a deployment and was still reeling from the stresses of her own experiences on the battlefield. On the day of the incident, Lily was at home, trying to decompress after her last mission. A call from her mother shattered this fragile calm when she learned about the accident. The news hit her like a freight train; it felt impossible that her brother could be gone so suddenly and without warning. The images of his smiling face at their last family gathering played over and over in her mind, leaving her feeling numb. Since then, Lily has struggled with intense discomfort whenever she is reminded of the event. Simple conversations about loss or seeing others discuss traumatic experiences trigger vivid recollections that feel like she's reliving it all over again. The memory replays so clearly that she feels as though she can see every detail-the look on her mother's face during the phone call, the sound of helicopters in the background, and the moment when she broke down. Her efforts to cope with these overwhelming memories have led her to suppress thoughts about the trauma, avoiding conversations about it whenever possible. She has become increasingly isolated, trying to avoid any potential triggers that might bring back those painful images. This avoidance extends beyond just talk; Lily avoids starting new relationships or friendships, believing that she can't rely on others and feeling a deep sense of defectiveness as a person. The weight of her brother's death is compounded by the guilt she feels for not being able to protect him. Despite knowing he was in training with skilled instructors, she still believes there was something more she could have done. This sense of failure has permeated every aspect of her life, including her occupation. Lily finds it increasingly difficult to fly missions or even interact with her squadron mates without feeling a pang of discomfort. Her avoidance behavior has strained her relationships at work; colleagues comment that she's become distant and less engaged in team activities. Lily's current state is marked by profound emotional distress and a growing sense of isolation. The weight of the memories and her negative appraisals have taken their toll on both her personal life and professional duties. She struggles to maintain focus during flights, haunted by the fear that she might fail someone else again. This has led to a noticeable decline in her performance, which is not lost on her superiors. What finally brought Lily to seek help was an incident at work where she nearly made a critical error due to her distracted state. Her commanding officer insisted she take time off and consider getting professional support. The thought of continuing this way, letting the memories consume her, terrifies her most. She is hopeful that through therapy, she might find a way to cope with these overwhelming thoughts and start rebuilding connections in both her personal and professional life. Lily's story reflects the complexity of living with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after such a profound loss. Her journey highlights the cyclical nature of symptoms-how avoidance can lead to isolation, how vivid memories can be triggered without warning, and how negative beliefs about oneself and others can exacerbate these experiences. Despite her struggles, there is a glimmer of hope that with support, she might find a path forward where she can manage her symptoms and reclaim some sense of control over her life.

Maria, a 19-year-old dancer of European descent, had experienced a man-made disaster that forever altered her life. The traumatic event occurred during a performance at a prestigious theater in New York City, where she was part of an ensemble dance group. During the show, a fire broke out unexpectedly, and the crowd panicked. Maria found herself trapped between the stage and a wall of people trying to escape. She was held down by the weight of others pushing against her as smoke filled the air. Since that night, Maria has been plagued by a variety of symptoms that have deeply impacted her life. Feeling very tired or exhausted is an everyday struggle for her, often leaving her drained and unable to focus on her rehearsals. The fear of being followed or tracked is ever-present, particularly when she walks alone through the bustling streets of New York City, where she lives. She also experiences a visceral reaction whenever she feels physically restrained or held down, which has made simple acts like hugging friends feel like threatening situations. Maria's coping mechanisms have been both maladaptive and damaging. She avoids going out as much as possible, staying locked in her apartment for days at a time. When she does venture outside, she often covers her face with her hands to avoid eye contact with others. This behavior has led to the gradual erosion of her social life and support network. Her passion for dance, once a source of joy and identity, is now something she avoids entirely, fearing it might trigger her traumatic memories. Maria's difficulties with concentration have become increasingly evident in her daily routine. She finds herself frequently distracted by intrusive thoughts about the fire, unable to focus on anything else. At night, she wakes up repeatedly, compelled to check whether she is safe. Her heightened startle response has also taken a toll; any unexpected movement nearby causes an intense reaction as if she were still in danger. The memory of that fateful evening feels incredibly vivid and real to Maria. She can relive the entire event through all her senses at once, with the smell of smoke lingering in her mind whenever she thinks about it. Despite knowing what happened, she struggles to articulate her experiences in words. This inability to fully express her trauma has compounded her sense of isolation. Maria's negative appraisals exacerbate her suffering. She feels that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing has been done to address the injustice. The thought of revisiting those memories is overwhelming, leading her to avoid thinking about the event altogether. This avoidance has left her feeling as though she no longer belongs anywhere. The culmination of these experiences finally pushed Maria to seek help. Her isolation had become unbearable, and she was desperate for a way out of this cycle of fear and exhaustion. She is most afraid that she will never feel safe again, but at the same time, she hopes that therapy can provide her with tools to manage her symptoms and reconnect with life. Maria's journey towards healing begins now, as she seeks support to navigate through the complex aftermath of trauma, hoping for a chance to reclaim her sense of belonging and joy in living.

James is a 57-year-old North American man who has been leading a solitary life since his traumatic experience. He works as a tutor, spending most of his days in libraries and small study rooms where he helps students with their homework and exam preparation. His trauma-a sexual assault-occurred several months ago and has left deep psychological scars that continue to affect his daily functioning. The attack happened one evening when James was walking home from work. He had stopped at a nearby park, intending only to rest on a bench for a moment before heading back to his apartment. It was there that he encountered the man who would assault him. The sudden and overwhelming physical force and loss of autonomy left an indelible mark on James. Since then, any form of physical touch or being in close proximity with men has become overwhelmingly triggering. James's daily routine is now a careful dance around his triggers and fears. He avoids situations that might evoke strong emotions, which he finds unsettling and overwhelming. His smoking habit has escalated as a coping mechanism, providing some semblance of comfort amidst the chaos of his thoughts. Any form of physical contact, even something as simple as a handshake or a pat on the back from a student, makes him feel exposed and vulnerable. In his role as a tutor, James finds himself increasingly isolated. He avoids being alone with male students for fear that it might trigger unwanted memories. This has led to some strained relationships at work; he has had to decline invitations to after-school events or collaborative study sessions where the presence of other men would be unavoidable. James's constant vigilance is palpable in his interactions and daily life. He watches others closely, constantly on the lookout for signs that they might harm him. This heightened state of alertness has made it difficult for James to trust anyone, leaving him feeling isolated and set apart from others. His choice of seating always reflects his need to feel safe; he positions himself in a corner where he can see everyone but remains out of reach. The vivid memory of the assault is ever-present in James's mind, with clear and detailed images that replay like a haunting movie. Yet, there are also gaps-times when memories feel incomplete, leaving him feeling fragmented and unsure about what truly happened. The inability to fully articulate his experience has left James feeling disconnected from others, as if he cannot adequately share or explain what haunts him. James's negative appraisals of himself and the world around him have become deeply ingrained. He no longer trusts his own body and feels that it betrayed him during the assault. His constant vigilance is a coping mechanism, but it has also led to an overwhelming sense of isolation and disconnection from others. What finally brought James to seek help was a particularly triggering incident at work. A male colleague had asked James to stay late to review some materials with a group of students, and James's fear and anxiety reached a breaking point. He realized that his life had become a series of avoidances, and he longed for the ability to reconnect with others without the constant fear of being harmed again. James is most afraid of never feeling safe again and living in perpetual isolation. However, he also hopes to find a way to reclaim some sense of normalcy and trust-both in himself and in those around him. His journey towards healing will involve navigating these fears while finding ways to rebuild his shattered sense of safety and trust.

John, a 30-year-old African-American man who works as a curriculum designer, had been struggling with his past for several months. The traumatic event that continues to haunt him was a period of severe physical abuse by his former romantic partner. This deeply painful experience left lasting marks on both his body and psyche. The night John remembers most vividly was one where the smell of alcohol permeated their apartment. His ex-partner had come home drunk, and the sharp acrid smell of burnt food from an overheated pan filled the kitchen. As he recalls this moment now, it's as if time has paused and the terror returns in full force. He can still feel the pain coursing through his body, the same parts that were bruised and broken during those attacks. John had come to believe that the person he once was is no longer recognizable to him. The man who faced his ex-partner with hope for a better future has been replaced by someone who constantly monitors their environment for potential threats. He feels deeply contaminated by what happened, as if there's an indelible mark on his being that can never be erased. The triggers are numerous and often unavoidable. Conversations about family life at work send waves of unease through him, particularly when colleagues casually mention their loving families or how they support each other. These comments remind John not only of the abuse he endured but also of the lack of familial support during those difficult times. He tries to avoid such conversations as much as possible, sometimes even excusing himself from meetings that might touch on these topics. John's daily life has become a series of small evasions and precautions. When walking home from work or out in public spaces, he is acutely aware of any scent reminiscent of alcohol or burnt food. Even the faintest whiff can bring back intense memories of that night, causing his heart to race and his hands to tremble. At times, when these triggers are particularly strong, John experiences a physical pain in the same areas where he was hurt during the abuse. The terror returns as vividly as it did then, leaving him feeling trapped by his own thoughts and sensations. These memories are not just abstract; they feel like real-time events replaying inside his mind. The injustice of what happened to John has become a pervasive theme in how he views the world. He feels that nothing has been done about his situation despite knowing that such abuse is deeply unfair. This sense of powerlessness and unresolved anger sometimes manifests as irritability at work, which has led to strained relationships with some colleagues. John had tried to carry on as normally as possible, but the accumulation of these triggers and memories began to take a toll. He found himself missing deadlines and becoming increasingly isolated from his coworkers. His performance reviews reflected this decline, and he was warned that further lapses could jeopardize his job security. What finally brought John to seek help was an incident at work where he had a panic attack during a presentation due to the accidental mention of family dynamics by one of his colleagues. The room went silent as he struggled to regain composure, but it only made things worse. After that day, John realized that continuing down this path would not lead to any meaningful recovery. In therapy, John hopes to address these triggers and memories in a safe space where he can begin to understand them without reliving the terror. He is most afraid of being forever trapped by his past but also holds onto hope for reclaiming parts of himself that feel lost. Through treatment, John aims to regain a sense of control over his life and find peace with his experiences.

James is a 36-year-old North American male who serves as a tax consultant in a bustling downtown office. Married and a veteran of the military, James has found that his service experiences have left indelible marks on his daily life. His PTSD symptoms emerged after a particularly harrowing deployment where he witnessed intense conflict and several close calls with death. The traumatic event began during a routine patrol when an unexpected explosion rocked their convoy. Amidst the chaos, James saw fellow soldiers injured and heard screams that seemed to echo through every corner of his mind. The taste of dust and gunpowder filled his mouth as he rushed to assist the wounded. This experience has left him deeply scarred, particularly by certain triggers like confrontations and specific conversation topics. James had come to believe that any form of physical contact with others was a potential threat. He would react with alarm if someone touched him unexpectedly, often pulling away reflexively. In his office, James found himself frequently startled when colleagues accidentally brushed past him or patted him on the back in camaraderie. These interactions left him feeling shaken and anxious, leading to avoidance behaviors that strained relationships at work. One day, while attending a mandatory team-building retreat, an unexpected handshake from a new colleague triggered an acute anxiety response. James felt his heart race and sweat form beads on his forehead. He quickly excused himself, retreating to the nearest bathroom where he could regroup and calm down. This incident marked one of many instances where James felt compelled to avoid any positive emotions because they made him feel unsafe. James had developed a habit of pushing away positive feelings due to a pervasive sense that something dangerous was always around the corner. He often found himself feeling numb, as if he were an observer rather than a participant in his own life. This emotional disconnection extended into his marriage, where he avoided deep conversations or meaningful interactions with his wife. In his daily routine, James would meticulously plan his days to include escape routes wherever he went. Whether it was the office building or a crowded coffee shop, he would carefully note every exit and entrance, feeling only secure once he had identified these potential escape paths. This behavior became particularly pronounced in public spaces where unexpected silence made him feel as if danger were imminent. James often experienced vivid flashbacks of the traumatic event, which were triggered by certain tastes that reminded him of the dust and gunpowder from the explosion. These memories would flood his mind with overwhelming emotions, leaving him feeling paralyzed and unable to continue his work or engage in social activities. At other times, he would recall the events but feel completely numb, as if they had happened to someone else. The impact on his marriage was significant. James avoided talking about the event or its aftermath with his wife, who felt increasingly isolated and disconnected from him. This avoidance not only strained their relationship but also exacerbated his own sense of isolation and fear. What finally brought James to seek help was a combination of escalating symptoms and the realization that he could no longer avoid the triggers that surrounded him daily. He had come to believe that if he continued on this path, his life would be forever compromised by his trauma. His greatest hope was to regain some sense of control over his emotions and relationships, to find a way to reconnect with his wife and colleagues without feeling perpetually threatened. In therapy, James expressed the fear that he might never fully recover from the event or that it could always intrude into his life unexpectedly. He hoped to learn strategies for managing his triggers and finding ways to engage in positive emotions again, reclaiming some sense of normalcy in his daily life.

Emily, a 33-year-old European-American graphic designer, has been living in a state of constant vigilance since she experienced a traumatic stalking incident over two years ago. Emily had moved to a new city for her job at a design firm and quickly found herself the target of an obsessive stalker who had begun following her on foot and even bicycling behind her as she rode home from work. The initial encounter began innocuously enough, with the man appearing to be just another cyclist on the path. However, over time, Emily noticed that he would consistently follow her route and seemed to take note of her schedule. Eventually, he started making explicit threats via social media, and Emily felt she was being watched everywhere she went. The trauma escalated when she found a threatening letter at her doorstep one morning, signed with the name "The Watcher." Since then, Emily has been hyper-aware of her surroundings, constantly scanning for signs that she is being followed or monitored. She avoids biking home from work and feels an overwhelming sense of dread whenever she rides past the locations where she encountered her stalker. The experience has left her feeling on edge, with a heightened startle response to even minor stimuli like sudden noises. Emily's world now revolves around avoiding places that remind her of the stalking incident. She no longer frequents the local park or café near her home, and whenever she goes out, she checks multiple times to ensure she isn't being followed. At work, Emily makes a point to stay close to the exit during meetings and always plans an escape route in case she feels unsafe. Her constant vigilance has made her feel isolated from others; she avoids social gatherings for fear of encountering someone who might remind her of her stalker. Despite her efforts to avoid triggering situations, Emily experiences frequent false alarms where she reacts as if she is in danger even when there are no actual threats present. These reactions have strained her relationships with colleagues and friends, who find it difficult to understand why she appears so anxious all the time. Her husband, Mark, has noticed a significant change in her behavior and expressed concern about how much the stalking experience has affected her. Emily's negative appraisals exacerbate her symptoms. She feels that the people responsible for the stalking have faced no consequences, leaving her with an overwhelming sense of injustice. The world now seems a dangerous place to her, where she cannot trust others easily. Emily is certain that everyone around her could be hiding malicious intentions, and this belief has made it difficult for her to form new relationships or even maintain existing ones. What frightens Emily most is the fear that this experience might define who she is moving forward-constantly looking over her shoulder, never truly feeling safe in any environment. She finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing incident at work where she felt overwhelmed and had to leave early due to an overwhelming sense of anxiety. Emily hopes therapy will help her regain some semblance of normalcy and trust in the world around her.

Carlos, a 54-year-old Latin American male and business owner, has been struggling with his mental health following his time as a relief worker in a war-torn region. His experiences have left deep scars that have slowly eroded his sense of safety and well-being over the past year. The traumatic event occurred during one of Carlos's missions to deliver supplies to civilians affected by ongoing conflict. Amidst the chaos, gunfire erupted near his vehicle, causing him to crash into a nearby ditch. The sound of bullets whizzing past his head and the sight of civilians running in terror were seared into his memory. Since then, any positive emotion, like hearing celebratory music or laughter, triggers an overwhelming sense of confusion and distress for Carlos. He finds himself jolted back to that moment, struggling to reconcile the joy he's supposed to feel with the fear he can't shake off. Over time, Carlos has developed a series of maladaptive strategies to cope with his symptoms. One of these is rumination; he often goes over and over why the event happened to him, seeking some sense of meaning or control in an otherwise incomprehensible situation. This constant replaying of events in his mind leaves him feeling exhausted and drained, as if he's reliving that moment every day. Another coping mechanism Carlos has adopted is carrying a weapon with him at all times. He carries it not just when he travels to high-risk areas but even while conducting business in the United States. This behavior is driven by a deep-seated belief that he must be prepared for any threat, no matter how unlikely or improbable it may seem. Carlos also finds himself engaging in conflict more frequently. He picks arguments with his staff and customers, often creating drama to distract himself from the trauma he carries. These conflicts have strained his relationships at work, leading to a decline in business performance and an increase in stress levels. His wife has noticed this shift as well, feeling increasingly isolated by her husband's volatile mood swings and constant preoccupation with danger. The combination of these symptoms has created a pervasive sense of unease for Carlos. The gunshot noise that once shattered his tranquility now seems to be lurking around every corner. Even the simple act of walking through crowded streets or being in physical proximity to others can trigger intense anxiety, leaving him feeling like he's constantly on edge. What frightens Carlos most is the fear of never truly finding peace again. He worries that these triggers and avoidance behaviors will continue to dominate his life, preventing him from fully engaging with his family and business. His wife has been urging him to seek help for months, noticing how his behavior has deteriorated over time. Finally, driven by her encouragement and a growing sense of desperation, Carlos decided it was time to reach out. Carlos is most hopeful that therapy can provide some relief and guidance on managing these overwhelming feelings. He hopes to regain control over his life, rebuild the relationships he's strained, and find ways to cope with his trauma without relying on harmful strategies. With this in mind, he has taken a significant step towards seeking help, knowing that recovery is possible if he commits to it. Through therapy, Carlos aims to understand why certain triggers are so potent for him, and how he can navigate them without resorting to destructive behaviors. He hopes to regain a sense of safety and balance in his life, one small step at a time.

Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has recently become widowed, has been working as a nanny in a suburban household since retiring from his previous job in retail. His life took an unexpected and harrowing turn when he witnessed the life-threatening illness of one of the children he was caring for-a young girl named Lily. The trauma began late one evening when Lily suddenly started convulsing and losing consciousness. Mr. Tran immediately called for emergency services, but during that time, he found himself frozen in fear and unable to act effectively. The ambulance eventually arrived, and Lily was rushed to the hospital where she spent several days in critical condition before slowly stabilizing. Since then, Mr. Tran has been struggling with a host of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. He avoids seeking medical care for himself, despite experiencing occasional chest pains and other concerning health issues. Each time he considers visiting a doctor, memories of Lily's convulsions flood back, leaving him feeling overwhelmed and frightened. This avoidance extends to psychological help as well; the thought of discussing his experiences is unbearable. Mr. Tran has also adopted a strategy of suppressing thoughts about the traumatic event. He tries hard not to think about what happened, often telling himself that he needs to focus on other things to keep his mind occupied. However, this constant mental distraction takes its toll. Mr. Tran finds himself frequently distracted at work, which has led to several minor mishaps and moments of forgetfulness, causing him some anxiety about maintaining the trust of the family he works for. Despite these efforts, his memories of Lily's illness remain vivid and feel more real than ordinary events in his life. He often relives those moments, feeling as though they are happening right now rather than something that is over. The memory of her convulsions triggers intense emotional responses whenever he sees anything similar-like a child having a minor seizure or even just falling down. Mr. Tran's sense of self has been deeply affected by this event. He feels unrecognizable to himself, believing that the person who once cared for children with joy and confidence is now someone who lives in constant fear and anxiety. This shift has made him distrustful of others, as he sees them not as supportive but as potentially dangerous or deceptive. His core belief is that he has permanently changed for the worse, and this conviction weighs heavily on his daily life. The combination of these symptoms and his increasing isolation have taken a toll on Mr. Tran's relationships with the family he works for. He avoids discussing any concerns about Lily's health out of fear it will trigger another episode, but this avoidance has led to misunderstandings and tension within the household. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was an incident where he became so overwhelmed by memories during a walk that he felt dizzy and disoriented. He realized that his constant attempts to avoid and suppress these experiences were no longer sustainable and that he needed professional support to navigate this challenging time in his life. Mr. Tran is most afraid of losing control over his own mind and emotions, feeling as though the trauma has fundamentally altered who he is. However, he also hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy and trust in himself and others. He wants to find a path forward that allows him to continue caring for children without being overwhelmed by the memories of Lily's illness.

Sai, a 46-year-old South Eastern Asian man, is a software engineer married to his high school sweetheart. These auditory memories replay like a film, making it nearly impossible for him to escape the trauma of those moments. He often feels as though he cannot verbalize what happened, leaving him with a sense of being trapped within these fragmented, non-verbal memories. Sai's hyperalertness has manifested in several ways. Even inside his own home, where he should feel safe, he remains on guard, constantly assessing the potential for danger. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because the unpredictability feels overwhelming; every stranger that approaches him makes him feel threatened, as if he is always on the lookout for another ambush. To cope with these intense feelings of vulnerability and fear, Sai has begun avoiding certain activities altogether. He no longer watches television or reads books, especially those related to combat scenarios, which can trigger unwanted memories and sensations. Exercise, once a regular part of his routine, now feels too risky; even the sound of motorcycle noise during his runs sends him spiraling into anxiety. Sai's avoidance has also seeped into his professional life as a software engineer. He finds it increasingly difficult to participate in team-building exercises or attend social gatherings that might take place outside familiar environments. This withdrawal from social and occupational activities has strained his relationships, particularly with colleagues who have noticed a change but cannot fully understand the depth of his distress. His marriage has also been affected. His wife worries about him but struggles to comprehend why he seems so distant and guarded. Sai's reluctance to discuss what happened in combat adds another layer of isolation; he feels that words are inadequate to describe the intensity of those experiences, leaving him feeling both trapped and misunderstood. What finally brought Sai to seek help was an incident where a motorcycle backfire at a local event triggered such intense anxiety that he had to leave abruptly, causing significant distress for his family. The overwhelming fear and the realization that this is affecting every aspect of his life have made him desperate for relief. He is most afraid of losing control completely and feels that seeking help might be the only way to reclaim some semblance of normalcy in his life. Sai hopes that therapy will provide a space where he can begin to make sense of these fragmented memories, learn to manage his triggers, and reconnect with the world outside his home without feeling constantly on edge. He is eager to regain control over his daily life and preserve the relationships that are most important to him.

John, a 28-year-old European American male, is a social media manager who has recently returned from military service. However, the reality of his deployment proved far more challenging than he anticipated. One of his closest friends suffered a devastating leg injury, and the sight of him being evacuated on a stretcher has stayed with John ever since. The sound of helicopters or aircraft can quickly plunge him into a state of high anxiety, reminiscent of the missions flown over rugged terrain. Driving with other people has become a source of significant distress for John, as it often reminds him of those tense moments on patrol when any vehicle could be a potential threat. This has led to his decision to avoid driving with others whenever possible, which has strained his relationship with his partner and colleagues who rely on him for carpooling. John's avoidance behaviors extend to military uniforms or weapons, which he now actively steers clear of. Even the sight of a police officer in uniform can trigger intense discomfort. He frequently rehearses what he will say before any social interaction, afraid that unexpected questions might expose his vulnerabilities.
